title: 00 — System Design: Chapter Notes Index
html:
00 — System Design: Chapter Notes Index

What this set is: one note per classic system-design problem, in the order the problems are usually taught — fundamentals first (scaling, estimation, a design-review framework), then building blocks (rate limiter, consistent hashing, KV store, ID generator), then full systems (URL shortener → stock exchange). How it differs from 08_SYSTEM_DESIGN_HLD: that file is the toolkit — the levers, the numbers, the vocabulary. This folder applies the toolkit to one problem at a time, the way a design review actually happens. Angle: every chapter ends with a .NET / Azure mapping, because knowing "use a message queue" is less useful than knowing "Service Bus sessions give you per-key ordering; Event Hubs gives you a replayable log".

1. The shape of every chapter

Every note follows the same four steps, because that is the order a good design conversation takes:

---
title: Chapter structure — four steps
---
flowchart LR
    A["Step 1<br/>Scope the problem<br/>requirements + numbers"] --> B["Step 2<br/>High-level design<br/>API, data, boxes"]
    B --> C["Step 3<br/>Deep dive<br/>the 2–3 hard parts"]
    C --> D["Step 4<br/>Wrap-up<br/>failures, trade-offs, what's next"]

Then two fixed sections: .NET / Azure mapping and Review checklist.

2. Chapter map

Part 1 — Foundations

# Chapter The one idea to take away
01 Scale from zero to millions Scale by removing state from the web tier, then by splitting the data tier
02 Back-of-the-envelope estimation Round aggressively; the order of magnitude is the answer
03 A framework for design reviews Requirements before boxes; deep-dive where the risk is

Part 2 — Building blocks

# Chapter The one idea to take away
04 Rate limiter Token bucket + a shared counter store; decide fail-open vs fail-closed
05 Consistent hashing Adding a node should move 1/n of the keys, not all of them
06 Key-value store Quorums (W + R > N) let you dial consistency against latency
07 Unique ID generator Snowflake: time + machine + sequence packs into 64 bits and sorts

Part 3 — Classic systems

# Chapter The one idea to take away
08 URL shortener ID → base62 beats hash-and-retry-on-collision
09 Web crawler The URL frontier is the design: politeness + priority queues
10 Notification system Queue per channel, retries, idempotency, user preferences
11 News feed Fan-out on write for normal users, on read for celebrities
12 Chat system Stateful WebSocket tier + a per-conversation ordered message store
13 Search autocomplete Precompute top-k per prefix; serve from memory; rebuild offline
14 Video platform (YouTube) Upload direct to blob storage, transcode as a DAG, serve from CDN
15 File sync (Google Drive) Split files into blocks; sync deltas; metadata needs strong consistency

Part 4 — Location and real-time

# Chapter The one idea to take away
16 Proximity service Geohash / quadtree turn 2-D search into 1-D prefix lookup
17 Nearby friends Location updates are ephemeral: pub/sub + cache, not a database
18 Maps and navigation Tile pyramids for rendering; hierarchical routing tiles for paths

Part 5 — Data-intensive infrastructure

# Chapter The one idea to take away
19 Distributed message queue Partitioned append-only log + consumer offsets
20 Metrics monitoring and alerting Time-series store, downsampling, alert rules evaluated off the hot path
21 Ad click aggregation Stream aggregation with event time, watermarks and reconciliation
22 Hotel reservation Inventory rows + optimistic locking; idempotent booking
23 Distributed email Metadata in a wide-column store, bodies in blob storage, search separate
24 S3-like object storage Separate metadata from data; erasure coding for durability per dollar
25 Real-time gaming leaderboard Redis sorted sets: O(log n) update and rank

Part 6 — Money

# Chapter The one idea to take away
26 Payment system Idempotency keys + a double-entry ledger + daily reconciliation
27 Digital wallet Balance transfers across shards need event sourcing or 2PC-style sagas
28 Stock exchange A single-threaded, in-memory, sequenced matching engine per symbol

3. How to study with this set

  1. Read 01–03 once, properly. Everything later assumes them.
  2. For each problem chapter, cover the page and do Step 1 and Step 2 yourself first — 10 minutes, paper, real numbers. Then read. The gap between your answer and the note is the thing to learn.
  3. Say the trade-offs out loud. Every chapter has a "Trade-offs" table; the reasoning is what reviewers remember, not the diagram.
  4. Cross-reference the toolkit when a chapter leans on a concept: caching and CAP → 08_SYSTEM_DESIGN_HLD, queues and outbox → 14_MESSAGING_AND_EVENT_DRIVEN, storage engines → 10_DATABASES_RELATIONAL / 11_DATABASES_NOSQL_AND_CACHING.

4. Further reading (primary sources)

Topic Source
Consistent hashing Karger et al., Consistent Hashing and Random Trees (1997); Google, Maglev (NSDI 2016)
Key-value stores Amazon, Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (SOSP 2007); Google, Bigtable (OSDI 2006)
Cassandra Lakshman & Malik, Cassandra — A Decentralized Structured Storage System (LADIS 2009)
Unique IDs Twitter Engineering, Announcing Snowflake (2010); Flickr, Ticket Servers (2010)
Crawling Olston & Najork, Web Crawling (Foundations and Trends in IR, 2010)
Chat Discord Engineering, How Discord Stores Billions of Messages
File sync Neil Fraser, Differential Synchronization (2009)
Message queues Kreps et al., Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing (2011)
Monitoring Facebook, Gorilla: A Fast, Scalable, In-Memory Time Series Database (VLDB 2015)
Stream processing Akidau et al., The Dataflow Model (VLDB 2015)
Payments Stripe Engineering, Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency
Circuit breakers Martin Fowler, CircuitBreaker (bliki)
